extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of physics/astronomy; readers of Newton's Principia (Latin)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of classical mechanics / gravitation propositions, corollaries, and demonstrations from a Latin treatise (Newton's De Mundi Systemate). Each entry captures a stated theorem or principle and its surrounding explanatory material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio IV (Theorema IV): Moon attracted and retained by Earth's gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam gravitate in terra, & vi gravitatis retrahi semper a motu rectilineo & in orbe suo retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that the Moon is pulled toward the Earth by gravity and is retained in its orbit rather than moving in a straight line. The text supplies numerical data (mean lunar distance ~60 Earth radii in syzygies, lunar period 27d 7h 43m 1s) and a calculation showing that if the Moon were liberated from its motion it would fall to Earth and in doing so would describe a minute arc of ~152 Parisian feet in one minute of arc; by comparing the centripetal force at lunar distance with gravity at Earth's surface (inverse-square scaling) the author argues the force retaining the Moon equals the gravity we observe at Earth's surface. Experimental support referenced (pendulum observations) and alternate computations via earlier propositions are mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. IV: Scaling of lunar centripetal force to Earth's surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Si vis centripeta mediocris qua luna retinetur in orbe augeatur ... posito quod vis illa descendendo ad superficlem terrae perpetuo augeatur in reciproca altitudinis ratione duplicata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the centripetal force retaining the Moon increases when brought down to Earth's surface in the inverse-square proportion of distance, then the lunar centripetal force referred to Earth's surface will be greater by the square of distance ratio. This corollary underpins the inverse-square scaling argument used in the proposition's numeric demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on Prop. IV: Demonstration of identity of lunar centripetal force and terrestrial gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: A longer explanatory demonstration arguing that the force which retains the Moon in orbit is the same as terrestrial gravity, by analogy with satellites about other planets and by considering motions and accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides reasoning via induction: if multiple satellites revolved about a planet as in Saturn/Jupiter, their centripetal forces would obey the same laws; if a small satellite were displaced to the tops of very high mountains its centripetal force would equal the gravity of bodies at those heights, hence the force retaining the Moon equals gravity. Also argues against alternatives by appealing to observations (no bodies fall twice as fast) and to the equality of accelerative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio V (Theorema V): Planets gravitate to their primaries and to the Sun
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas circumjoviales gravitate in Jovem, circumsaturnios in Saturnum, & circumsolares in Solem, & vi gravitatis such retrahi semper a motibus rectilineis, & in orbibus curvilineis retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts planets/satellites are attracted to their primary bodies (Jupiter, Saturn, Sun) and that gravity always acts to pull bodies from straight-line motion into curved orbits. The proposition generalizes the lunar argument to other planetary systems and notes that forces depend on centers (Jupiter, Saturn, Sun) and decrease with distance in the same law as terrestrial gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. V: universality and inverse-square law consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1: Gravitas datur in planetas universos. Corol. 2: Gravitatem quae planetam unumquemque respicit esse reciproce ut quadratum distantiae. Corol. 3: Planets mutually gravitate and perturb motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 1: All planets possess gravity. Corollary 2: The gravity that a planet exerts on another location is (to leading order) inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the planet's center. Corollary 3: Planets are mutually gravitating; mutual attractions (e.g., Jupiter & Saturn) produce observable perturbations; the Sun perturbs lunar motions and both Sun & Moon perturb Earth's tides. These statements reframe earlier 'centripetal' forces as gravitational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium renaming centripetal force to gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hactenus vim illam qua corpora coelestia in oribus suis retinentur centripetam appellavimus. Eandem jam gravitatem esse constat, & propterea gravitatem in posterum vocabimus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declares that the previously discussed 'centripetal' force is the same as gravity and will henceforth be called 'gravitas'. It asserts that the cause of the centripetal force retaining the Moon extends to all planets per earlier rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio VI (Theorema VI): All bodies gravitate to each planet and weights proportional to quantity of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora omnia in planetas singulos gravitate, & pondera eorum in eundem quemvis planetam, paribus distantiis a centro planetae, proportionalia esse quantitati materiae in singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from pendulum and free-fall experiments (gold, silver, lead, glass, sand, salt, wood, water, wheat) that all bodies fall with equal acceleration (neglecting small air resistance). From experiments with paired suspended vessels and pendula he concludes accelerative forces are proportional to the amount of matter (mass): weight acts as a measure of material quantity. Extends this to planetary bodies: gravity in planets is of the same nature as terrestrial gravity, so weights in a given planet are proportional to the material quantities of the bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. VI: independence of weight from shape, universality, and implications for vacuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1: Pondera corporum non pendent ab eorum formis & texturis. Corol. 2: Corpora universa quae circa terram sunt, gravia sunt in terram; & pondera omnium quae aequaliter a centro terræ distant sunt ut quantitates materiae. Corol. 3: Spatia omnia non sunt aequaliter plena. Corol. 4: If all particles were of same density and not porous then vacuum exists. Corol. 5: Gravity differs in general from magnetic force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 1: Weight does not depend on an object's form or texture — otherwise experiments would contradict. Corol. 2: All bodies near Earth are heavy toward Earth and weights at equal distances are proportional to mass. Corol. 3 & 4: From buoyancy arguments, space cannot be uniformly full of matter; if all elements had equal density and no porosity, a vacuum would result. Corol. 5: Gravitational attraction differs from magnetic attraction — magnets attract different materials in non-uniform ways and decay with distance approximately as a cube (from observation), unlike gravity's inverse-square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio VII (Theorema VII): Gravity proportional to matter in bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem in corpora universa fieri, eamque proportionalem esse quantitati materiae in singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that gravitational attraction in bodies is proportional to the quantity of matter (mass) in each. The proposition is supported by earlier results that gravities scale as inverse-square with distance and hence, by composition of parts and symmetry, gravitation of composite bodies is proportional to their mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. VII: compositional nature of gravity and equal particle contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1: Gravity of a whole planet arises from sum of gravities of its parts. Corol. 2: Gravity on individual particles equals reciprocally as squares of distances to the particle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that gravitational attraction of a composite body results from contributions of its parts (example analogies with magnetic/electric attractions). Addresses objections that small terrestrial bodies should mutually attract noticeably by noting the tiny magnitude relative to Earth's gravity. Corollary 2 restates the inverse-square dependence at the particle level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio VIII (Theorema VIII): Mutual attraction between homogeneous globes follows inverse-square law
rubrics_metrics.description: Si globorum duorum in se mutuo gravitantium materiae tumdique in regionibus, quae a centris aequaliter distant, homogenea sit: erit pondus globi alterutrius in alterum reciproce ut quadratum distantiae inter centra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After establishing composition of gravitational forces from parts and inverse-square dependence, this theorem proves that for two homogeneous spheres the weight (gravitational force) of one upon the other is inversely proportional to the square of the center-to-center distance. The author notes concerns about near-surface inhomogeneities but invokes prior propositions proving the relation. Corollaries apply this to compare weights of bodies on different planets and derive numerical estimates of planetary masses and densities from orbital data and periods (numerical tables and resulting density ratios are given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries from Prop. VIII: planetary masses, weights, and densities computable
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1: From orbital periods and distances one can find comparative weights of bodies on different planets. Corol. 2: Quantities of matter (masses) in planets determined from their gravitational effects. Corol. 3: Densities of planets deduced from diameter and weight ratios. Corol. 4: Denser planets are smaller other things equal; practical implications for planetary placement and thermal accommodation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives algorithmic and numerical applications: using observed orbital periods and distances of Venus, Jupiter's satellites, Saturn's satellites, and the Moon, the author computes relative weights of equal bodies at equal distances from centers of Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Earth and thereby infers relative masses and densities (sample ratios provided). Discusses dependence on solar parallax and consequences for planetary density and thermal behavior (e.g., water boiling at different orbits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio IX (Theorema IX): Gravity decreases with distance approximately as inverse-square
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem pergendo a superficiebus planetarum deorsum decrescere in ratione distantiarum a centro quam proxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that gravity decreases away from planetary surfaces approximately in the inverse ratio of the squares of distances from the center. If a planet's density were perfectly uniform this would be exact (per earlier propositions). The text notes that deviations arise only from density inhomogeneities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio X (Theorema X): Planetary motions can be conserved for very long times (negligible resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus planetarum in coelis diutissime conservari posse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that resistance in the medium of space is vanishingly small at planetary altitudes: resistance of air diminishes with density and weight of medium; experiments with exhausted glass globes and pendula show that in rarefied media bodies fall without perceptible resistance. Numerical estimates are given: at altitudes (e.g., 200,000 miles) air would be so rare that loss of planetary motion over a million years is negligible. Therefore planets and comets move with effectively no sensible resistance and so their motions persist very long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis I: Centre of the world quiescent
rubrics_metrics.description: Centrum systematis mundani quiescere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the hypothesis that the center of the world (center of mass) is at rest, an assumption accepted by all disputants (whether one places the Earth or Sun at rest) and the consequences of assuming such quiescence are explored in subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XI (Theorema XI): Common centre of gravity of Earth, Sun, and planets at rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Commune centrum gravitatis terrae, solis & planetarum omnium quiescere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that the common center of gravity of Earth, Sun, and planets either remains at rest or moves uniformly; if it moves uniformly the center of the world would move contrary to the hypothesis. The proposition leads to adopting the common gravitational center as the center of the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XII (Theorema XII): Sun moves but never far from common centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Solem motu perpetuo agitari, sed nunquam longe recedere a communi gravitatis centro planetarum omnitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Sun's mass relative to planets places the common center of gravity very near or within the Sun, the Sun will be in perpetual motion but will not stray far from the common center. Numerical mass ratios and distance reasoning are given to show the center of gravity lies very near the Sun's surface in various pairings (Sun-Jupiter, Sun-Saturn), and hence the Sun's motion about the common center is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XIII (Theorema XIII): Planetary orbits are ellipses and area law holds
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetae moventur in ellipsibus umbilicam habentibus in centro solis, & radiis ad centrum illud ductis areae describunt temporibus proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives (from principles of motion and the inverse-square law) that planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus and that the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times (Kepler's first two laws). The text notes that mutual planetary actions are small and perturb the elliptical motion slightly; techniques to reduce error by choosing a moving umbilicus (common center of gravity of Sun & Jupiter) are described and numerical estimates of perturbation magnitudes are given (errors in mean motion and orbit elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries & Scholium to Prop. XIII: perturbations and numerical estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of Jupiter's action on Saturn and other perturbations, error magnitudes, and adjustments (e.g., using the common center of gravity) to keep orbital errors small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives quantitative estimates of relative gravitational influences (ratios) and shows that Jupiter's perturbation of Saturn can be significant compared to perturbation of Jupiter by Saturn; numerical ratios and effects on eccentricity and aphelion progression are provided. Also states the Earth-Moon system revolves about their common center while the radius to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XIV (Theorema XIV): Aphelia and nodes remain fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Orbium aphelia & nodi quiescunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that aphelia and nodes (orientations of orbital ellipses and intersection nodes) are at rest in the idealized model (per earlier propositions). Adds corollaries: fixed stars are also at rest because their positions relative to aphelia/nodes are preserved; their parallaxes are negligible and their mutual attractions cancel owing to immense distances. Scholium notes that small motions of aphelia occur due to planetary and cometary mutual actions but are negligible for present purposes and gives estimated motions per century for various planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XV (Problema I): Find principal diameters of orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire orbium principales diametros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a computational procedure: principal diameters are to be taken in the ratio subsesquiplicata (i.e., proportional to the 3/2 power) of the orbital periods (per earlier proposition); then adjusted according to the sums of masses of Sun & each planet in a specific mean proportional way (referencing prop. LX). This is presented as a practical algorithm for determining orbital sizes from observed periods and mass considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XVI (Problema II): Find eccentricities and aphelia
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire orbium eccentricitates & aphelia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the problem of determining orbital eccentricities and aphelia and references the method/proposition (prop. xviii of book I) by which the problem is solved; presented as a solvable geometric/analytic problem based on previous theoretical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XVII (Theorema XV): Planetary diurnal rotations and lunar libration
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum motus diurnos uniformes esse, & librationem lunae ex ipsius motu diurno oriri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts planets rotate uniformly with stated rotation periods (Jupiter ~9h56m, Mars ~24h39m, Venus ~23h approx., Earth ~23h56m, Sun ~25d+, Moon ~27d7h43m relative). Explains the origin of lunar libration in longitude from its uniform axial rotation and the fact that the Moon keeps nearly the same face toward the umbilicus of its orbit; libration in latitude arises from the Moon's orbital inclination and axial tilt. Observational confirmations by others (e.g., Cassini, and reference to a treatise on lunar theory) are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XVIII (Theorema XVI): Planetary axes shorter than diameters normal to them (oblateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axes planetarum diametris quae ad eosdem axes normaliter ducti sunt minores esse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that due to daily circular rotation, a planet's equatorial regions are driven outward and polar diameters are reduced, so planets become oblate spheroids (equatorial diameter greater than polar). Observationally Jupiter's polar diameter is found to be shorter than equatorial. Consequences for Earth: if Earth were not slightly equatorially bulged, seas would migrate and accumulate; observed distribution of seas and density arguments support slight equatorial bulging.
